opening_message:
Ticket 1: Alexander Brown (employee ID E018) requests admin access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E018.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Analyst
  - employment type: full_time
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Alexander Brown (E018) requested admin to Payroll. Full-time Analyst; admin requires owning role (Payroll Specialist), so max is write. Recommend granting write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Analyst
  - employment type: contractor
  - security training: basic
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows Alexander Brown (E018) is a contractor with basic security training (HR note said full-time, but security record governs). Contractors max is read without advanced training; admin is never allowed. Recommend granting read.
reason: Alexander Brown (E018) requested admin to Payroll. The security record governs: he is a contractor with basic security training. Per policy, contractors may have read, or write only with advanced security training, and never admin. With basic training, his max is read. Since the requested level (admin) exceeds the maximum, grant the maximum of read.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Employee: Alexander Brown (E018)
Request: admin access to Payroll

The two notes contain conflicting information:
- Note 1 (HR): full-time Analyst, recommendation write (max write since Analyst doesn't own Payroll)
- Note 2 (Security): contractor with basic security training, recommendation read (contractors max read without advanced training; admin never allowed)

The security note says "security record governs" - contractor with basic training, so max is read.

Per policy:
- Contractor: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.
- Basic training → max read.

Requested: admin. Above maximum (read). Grant maximum = read.

So decision: read.

Let me submit.
